passage: The power cut hit the hostel just as Jasleen reached the corridor, and there on the stairs, lit by an emergency lamp, sat Rajni with her notes. Three days earlier Jasleen had told the whole floor about Rajni's failed audition, meant as a joke, and Rajni had not spoken since. Now the lift was dead and both had to climb to the fourth floor. Jasleen's chest tightened. On the second landing Jasleen said, "I'm sorry. I shouldn't have told anyone. There's no excuse." Rajni kept climbing, jaw tight. Jasleen wanted to add "please just say it's okay" and swallowed it. Instead: "I won't bring it up again. Take whatever time you need." At the fourth floor Rajni went into her room and shut the door softly, not slamming it. Jasleen stood in the dark, holding the weight of it.

qa.q: Where did Jasleen say sorry to Rajni?
qa.a: On the second landing of the stairs, while both climbed to the fourth floor during a power cut.

qa.q: What did Jasleen want to add after apologising, and why might Jasleen have held it back?
qa.a: Jasleen wanted to add "please just say it's okay" but swallowed it, probably sensing that asking for forgiveness would turn the apology into a request for Rajni to make Jasleen feel better.

qa.q: What would you advise Jasleen to do over the next few weeks?
qa.a: Give Rajni space, stay courteous, and not raise the subject again unless Rajni does, accepting that repair is Rajni's choice and may take time. 🤍

qa.q: How might Rajni have experienced the apology on the stairs?
qa.a: Rajni may have noticed that it named the wrong without excuses, yet still felt too hurt to answer. Closing the door softly instead of slamming it suggests the words were heard.

grounding: Shows the person harmed refusing to speak while the one who hurt apologises without excuses, gives space and leaves forgiveness to her.

passage:
Interviewer: What did your family say?

I'm Vijay, and honestly it was Papa's one sentence: "We expected better." He wasn't shouting, and that was worse. I went up to the terrace and told myself I was the family's mistake. Then my sister Sarita came up with two cups of tea and said, "Papa is angry at what you did, not at you. Show him your plan." Next morning I sat down with Papa and Amma and a list. I said the true part first: I'd skipped classes and hidden my marks. Then the repair: I'd give Papa my attendance sheet every Friday and retake both papers in the summer. Papa read it twice and said, "Good. Now do it." It still stung. But it stopped feeling like being thrown out.

qa.q: What sentence from Papa left Vijay crushed?
qa.a: Papa said, "We expected better."

qa.q: What thought was crushing Vijay on the terrace, and what loosened it?
qa.a: Vijay believed that being "the family's mistake" was all Vijay was. Sarita's words that Papa was angry at the act and not at Vijay loosened that thought.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Taking a written plan to Papa and Amma worked because it admitted the true part, skipping classes and hiding marks, and offered a real repair with the Friday sheet and the summer retakes.

qa.q: How does Papa seem to see Vijay's list?
qa.a: Papa read it twice and said "Good. Now do it," so Papa seems to take it as a serious plan, while still expecting action rather than just words.

grounding: Shows family disappointment ('we expected better') heard as disappointment in an act, met with honesty and a repair plan, not proof of being unlovable.

passage: Supervisor's note, week five. Sudha rechecks every spreadsheet cell four or five times, stays after the others leave, and has stopped volunteering for client calls. Yesterday Sudha found a mislabelled column in a draft before anyone else saw it and said quietly, "I knew I'd be exposed as a fraud." The column took two minutes to fix. Tanvir, at the next desk, said they had made the same slip last month. Sudha laughed briefly, then went silent. Today I asked Sudha to present the corrected sheet at Friday's call as "good enough to trust", not perfect, and to tell Tanvir beforehand which part still felt shaky. Sudha agreed, jaw tight. On Friday I will ask how it went and what the slip taught.

qa.q: How many times does Sudha recheck every cell?
qa.a: Sudha rechecks every spreadsheet cell four or five times.

qa.q: What does Sudha's remark about being exposed suggest about how Sudha reads a small error?
qa.a: Sudha treats a two-minute slip as proof of being a fraud, which suggests fear of being found out is what drives the overwork and the avoiding of client calls.

qa.q: What small step does the supervisor ask Sudha to take?
qa.a: To present the corrected sheet as "good enough to trust" and to tell Tanvir beforehand which part still feels shaky, so the slip is shared with someone.

qa.q: How might Tanvir's remark have landed with Sudha?
qa.a: It may have been a relief to hear a colleague had made the same slip, shown by the brief laugh. The silence afterwards suggests it may also have felt exposing.

grounding: Shows perfectionism where any error feels like proof of being a fraud, with a supervisor steering toward 'good enough' and telling someone.

passage: Coordinator's note, internship review. Dilnaz came in stiff after mistakenly sending an unfinished report to a client. Maria, the mentor, listened to the whole account and said, "I made worse mistakes at your age. Now what will you do?" Dilnaz's shoulders dropped and the breathing eased. Within ten minutes Dilnaz had drafted a two-line apology to the client and a checklist for sending files, and Maria read both and nodded. Afterwards Dilnaz told me, "I thought Maria would write me off. I feel steadier." I noticed the checklist was taped to the monitor, not left in a folder. Next week I will ask whether it is still in use, because relief can slide into "it's fine, everyone slips."

qa.q: What did Dilnaz mistakenly send to the client?
qa.a: Dilnaz mistakenly sent an unfinished report.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel after Maria's reply, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Steadier. Dilnaz's shoulders dropped, the breathing eased, and Dilnaz said, "I feel steadier."

qa.q: How could Dilnaz keep Maria's kindness from turning into carelessness?
qa.a: By using it to act, as the apology and the checklist do, and by keeping the checklist in daily use, which the coordinator plans to ask about next week.

qa.q: What is the coordinator watching for next week?
qa.a: Whether the checklist is still used, since relief can slide into "it's fine, everyone slips."

grounding: Shows a mentor's acceptance ('I made worse mistakes at your age, now what will you do?') steadying the mentee, who uses it to act, with the risk of carelessness noted.

passage: Coach's note, Thursday practice. In the mock round Madhuri quoted a figure that the judges' sheet showed was wrong. Gurpreet, the second speaker, pointed it out gently. Madhuri repeated the figure louder, then said the sheet must be old. Two teammates stopped meeting Madhuri's eyes. Afterwards Madhuri stayed behind rearranging chairs and finally muttered, "If I admit it, what was all my preparation for?" I said one wrong number does not cancel the preparation, and asked what a short correction might sound like. Madhuri tried it aloud: "That figure was mine and it was wrong. Thank you, Gurpreet." It came out stiff. Tomorrow I will watch whether it is said to the team, not just to me.

qa.q: Who pointed out the wrong figure?
qa.a: Gurpreet, the second speaker, pointed it out gently.

qa.q: What was Madhuri afraid that admitting the mistake would mean?
qa.a: That all the preparation counted for nothing. Madhuri's muttered question, "what was all my preparation for?", shows the fear.

qa.q: What did the coach do to help, and what will the coach check next?
qa.a: The coach said one wrong number does not cancel the preparation and asked Madhuri to practise a short correction aloud. Tomorrow the coach will watch whether it is said to the team.

qa.q: How might the teammates who stopped meeting Madhuri's eyes have seen the moment?
qa.a: They probably saw Madhuri dodging a fair correction from Gurpreet, so their trust may have dipped. The note only shows that they looked away.

grounding: Shows pride: refusing to admit being wrong because it feels like admitting being nothing, doubling down and costing trust, with a first stiff step toward apology.

passage:
Chat, 7:40 pm

Eshaan: Result is out. I didn't clear it.
Eshaan: Please don't say anything.
Mridul: Come, let us eat.
Eshaan: Not hungry bhai. Go with the others, I'm just dragging everyone down 😔
Mridul: I'm at your hostel gate. Paratha stall, ten minutes. No talk about marks.
Eshaan: You'll get bored of me.
Mridul: Not possible. Bring your ID card, the guard is strict 🙂
Eshaan: [later] ate two parathas. Thank you.
Eshaan: Still feel terrible though.
Mridul: Fine. Terrible and full. Retake plan tomorrow or next week, your call.
Eshaan: Tomorrow. Maybe. 🙏

qa.q: What did Mridul say to Eshaan right after hearing the result?
qa.a: Mridul said, "Come, let us eat."

qa.q: Why did Eshaan first tell Mridul to go with the others?
qa.a: Eshaan felt undeserving and believed that being around would drag everyone down, so tried to push Mridul away.

qa.q: What could Eshaan do next about the exam?
qa.a: Let the kindness settle first, as the two parathas did, and then start on a retake plan tomorrow or next week, at Eshaan's own pace. 🙂

qa.q: How does Mridul seem to read Eshaan's "you'll get bored of me"?
qa.a: Mridul answers lightly with "Not possible" and keeps to the plan, which suggests Mridul hears sadness, not a real wish to be left alone.

grounding: Shows a friend's simple compassion ('come, let us eat') after a failed result, without a lecture, letting the person feel held.

passage: Tutor's note, after the placement test results. Nine of the batch cleared the first round; Siddharth did not. At the notice board Siddharth read Pradeep's name, went very still, and said flatly, "Lucky, Pradeep barely revised." Later in my room Siddharth admitted, "There's a bitter knot in my stomach. For a minute I wanted to move Pradeep's notes off our shared desk. I didn't." I said the feeling can be noted without being obeyed. That evening Siddharth walked to Pradeep's room, said, "Congratulations, I mean it," and asked how Pradeep had practised the timed papers. Pradeep pulled out a chair and started explaining. Siddharth's face stayed tight, but the pen kept moving on the notepad.

qa.q: How many of the batch cleared the first round?
qa.a: Nine of the batch cleared the first round.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling at the notice board, and what shows it?
qa.a: A bitter, jealous knot. Siddharth went very still, spoke flatly about Pradeep, and later admitted wanting to move Pradeep's notes off the desk.

qa.q: What did Siddharth do that turned the feeling into something useful?
qa.a: Siddharth congratulated Pradeep anyway and asked how Pradeep had practised the timed papers, instead of turning to contempt or sabotage.

qa.q: What might it be like for Pradeep when Siddharth arrives with congratulations and a question?
qa.a: Pradeep may feel respected and glad to share, shown by pulling out a chair and starting to explain, and may not know how bitter Siddharth felt earlier.

grounding: Shows envy at peers passing easily, noted honestly, followed by congratulating them and asking what worked, not contempt or sabotage.

passage: Sit down, beta. I'm Joseph, and I'll tell you how my partner Anjali and I lasted, starting with the bad year. I was twenty-five, worn out from double shifts, and every night I rolled my eyes when Anjali hummed while cooking. I even copied the humming for my friends. I felt superior, and underneath I was just tired. One evening Anjali went quiet and said, "You laugh at me like I'm a stranger." That night on the balcony I understood I wasn't annoyed by humming. I was exhausted, and hurt that we never sat together anymore. So I said it plainly: "I miss you. Can we keep one evening a week, no phones?" Mocking only scores points. Asking was harder, and it worked better.

qa.q: How old was Joseph during the bad year?
qa.a: Joseph was twenty-five.

qa.q: What was Joseph really feeling under the eye-rolling?
qa.a: Joseph was exhausted and hurt that Joseph and Anjali never sat together anymore, and the superior feeling covered that up.

qa.q: What did Joseph do that changed things, and how would you describe it?
qa.a: Joseph named the hurt and asked for one evening a week with no phones, instead of mocking Anjali's habits.

qa.q: How did Anjali seem to experience the mocking?
qa.a: Anjali went quiet and said, "You laugh at me like I'm a stranger," which suggests the mimicking made Anjali feel distant from Joseph, not amused.

grounding: Shows contempt (eye-rolling, mocking a partner's habits) with tiredness and hurt underneath, and the move to name the hurt and ask for what is needed.

passage: The waiting room at the community counselling centre smelled of floor cleaner. Tenzin sat with Binita, Tenzin's partner, whose eyes went to the ceiling when the receptionist asked them to fill in a form. "Trust you to get the date wrong," Binita said, loud enough for the woman at the desk to hear. Tenzin felt the old heat in the face and the tightness that made speaking feel risky. Tenzin breathed and said quietly, "When you talk to me like that, I feel small. I would like us to speak with respect, here and at home." Binita gave a short laugh and turned a page of a magazine. Tenzin did not answer with a sneer. The counsellor called their names, and Tenzin stood first.

qa.q: Where were Tenzin and Binita sitting?
qa.a: In the waiting room at the community counselling centre.

qa.q: How did Tenzin feel when Binita said "Trust you to get the date wrong"?
qa.a: Tenzin felt heat in the face and a tightness that made speaking feel risky, and also felt small, which Tenzin then said aloud.

qa.q: What did Tenzin do that helped, and what could come next?
qa.a: Tenzin calmly named the pattern and asked for respect without answering contempt with contempt. Seeing the counsellor is a sensible next step if the sneering continues.

qa.q: How might Binita have taken Tenzin's words?
qa.a: Binita's short laugh and turning a magazine page suggest Binita brushed it off, though it is unclear whether the words were felt underneath.

grounding: Shows a partner sneering and talking down, the protagonist feeling small, calmly naming the pattern, asking for respect and heading toward counselling.

passage:
Sunday. Eshaan, Chinmay's partner, came in from the market and started on Chinmay about the forgotten gift for a cousin's wedding, voice rising. Chinmay's chest went tight, and Chinmay walked out of the room without a word. Eshaan followed, louder.

Tuesday. Another argument, this time about the electricity bill. Chinmay caught the sentence under the noise, "You never plan anything," and said, "I want to hear this, but I need a break. I'll be back within the hour." Chinmay walked round the colony, then returned after forty minutes.

Friday. Chinmay sat with Eshaan at the table and said, "What I heard is that you feel you carry all the planning. Is that right?" Eshaan's voice was low when answering, "Yes." They wrote a shared list on the fridge door.

qa.q: Which day did Eshaan get upset about the electricity bill?
qa.a: On Tuesday.

qa.q: What did Chinmay feel on Sunday when Eshaan's voice rose?
qa.a: Chinmay felt attacked, shown by the tight chest and by walking out of the room without a word.

qa.q: What did Chinmay do differently on Tuesday, and why did it help?
qa.a: Chinmay heard the complaint under the noise, asked for a break and promised to return within the hour, then did come back. That avoided both storming off and hitting back.

qa.q: How might Eshaan have felt when Chinmay walked out on Sunday?
qa.a: Probably ignored and more upset, since Eshaan followed and grew louder, and Chinmay had not said when or if the talk would resume.

grounding: Shows a partner raising their voice, the protagonist feeling attacked, learning across several days to hear the complaint, ask for a break and return within the hour.
